excerpt_en: Rewatching Bunny Girl Senpai after a solo trip to Japan — Kamakura's sea, a stranger chasing Sakurajima Mai, a girl in Osaka I can never contact again — and why I refuse a life lived by timetable.
body_en:
These past few days, I watched Rascal Does Not Dream of Bunny Girl Senpai again.

The first time I opened it, I was still in middle school. I just thought the title was bizarre — a pig-headed boy, a bunny girl senpai, like words someone had thrown together at random. I was young, I saw nothing special in it, and once the excitement was over, that was that.

This time, I understood something else: the Puberty Syndrome. All those feelings that can't be said out loud, all those moments when the mood around you pushes you along and you don't dare speak up even though you don't want to — the anime lays them out, one by one. And the more I watched, the more I felt my own story had to start with that trip to Japan at the beginning of 2026.

The First Time I Saw the Sea

At the start of 2026, I flew to Japan alone.

Half the reason was that I wanted to see with my own eyes what a society with democratic politics actually looks like. The other half was that I wanted to stand somewhere nobody knew me, and make a choice for my future self.

I walked alone along the shore at Kamakura. It was the first time in my life I had ever seen the sea. When you grow up inland, everything you imagine about the ocean comes from a screen: the "boundless waves" in textbooks, the surf and sunsets in videos. Standing on the edge of Sagami Bay with the wind in my face, I learned that "endless" is not an adjective. It presses down on you.

A Sunset at Enoshima, and a Countryman Whose Name I Never Learned

The sunset at Enoshima was beautiful, and I wanted someone to take a photo for me.

Looking around, I spotted a guy holding a Huawei phone. Abroad, that is probably the most reliable compatriot detector there is. I went up and asked. Sure enough, he was Chinese.

He was from Henan, studying civil engineering at Xi'an Jiaotong University. He told me he had flown to Japan alone too, for the simplest of reasons: he loves Sakurajima Mai, and he wanted to see the Kamakura where Sakuta and Mai live — to chase something he loves.

Two young Chinese men who never learned each other's names, brought together by an anime, pressing the shutter for each other on a foreign shore, then scattering into the crowd. I still don't know his name. But I remember exactly what the sunset looked like as it sank beside Mount Fuji that day.

February 6, Osaka

On February 6, I was changing trains in Osaka, from the Keihan Main Line to the Osaka Loop Line, on my way to drop my luggage at the hotel.

I couldn't make sense of the transfer rules at all, and the station was surging with people. With my few phrases of Japanese and my broken English, I asked a girl who looked like a high school student for help. She warmly told me, in English, that she was going the same way and I should follow her. I trailed awkwardly behind her, squeezing against the flow of the crowd.

She asked where I was from. In a mix of English and Japanese I said: China, and that I was headed toward Kansai Airport. I showed her the photos from beneath Mount Fuji. She said Fuji was beautiful, and that she had never left Osaka. When the conversation got too complicated for words, we pulled out our phones and talked through a translation app. She had an iPhone too; the two phones touched, and her contact card shared itself over automatically.

She walked me to the ticket gate — but she never entered the Osaka Loop Line herself. It was never her line to take. She had gone out of her way to bring me there. We waved goodbye, and I said goodbye to her in Japanese.

After I came home, I changed my SIM card, and her contact card was lost. We never had the chance to reach each other again. In iMessage there is still one message from her, with a photo attached — me, just after I had passed through the gate, taken from behind without my knowing. My replies can no longer be delivered.

That conversation window just stops there.

Life by Timetable

After I came home, I opened Bunny Girl Senpai again.

Only this time did I truly get it: the people in anime are allowed to live for their own lives. They can choose the person they want to love. They can charge ahead, heedless, toward a future that belongs to them.

Real Japanese high school students are the same. School lets out early in the afternoon, and they take photos at Tsurugaoka Hachimangu and the Great Buddha of Kamakura, and go after the things they love. Their time is their own.

And us?

We Chinese — millions upon millions of us, mass-produced like products on an assembly line — have no choices of our own. High school, university, a job, marriage: every station of life has its timetable printed in advance, and all you have to do is appear on the right platform at the right time. Nobody asks where you want to go, because the route was decided for you long ago.

Twenty Years Old, and Still Not Cured

Maybe all of this is just another form of Puberty Syndrome.

But I am already twenty. I am long past puberty. It's just that the part of me that went missing — making one choice for myself, living once for the people and things I love — will not grow back on its own with age. Healing it may take a whole lifetime.

That is also why I am so determined to go to America, and to take my fate into my own hands.

The tide at Kamakura is still coming in. My puberty arrived late. But it arrived.
